title: Queue
summary: First in, first out. Add at the back, remove from the front — the shape of fairness, of buffering, and of exploring level by level.

analogy.beginner: A queue at a ticket counter. You join at the back; the person who has been waiting longest is served next. Nobody jumps in at the middle. That is the entire rule.
analogy.interview: A FIFO collection with O(1) enqueue and dequeue. Implemented as a circular buffer over an array (head and tail indices wrapping with modulo) or a linked list with head and tail pointers. Java: `ArrayDeque` for general use, `LinkedList` when you need `List` semantics too, `ArrayBlockingQueue` for producer/consumer.

intuition:
A queue is the data structure of *waiting in order* — and, less obviously, of *breadth*.

The FIFO rule means every item is processed in arrival order, which is what makes a queue the right tool for fairness (job scheduling), for smoothing bursts (buffering), and for decoupling a fast producer from a slow consumer (message queues — see the System Design track, where the same idea reappears at the scale of whole services).

The algorithmic use is subtler. If you explore a graph or tree using a queue, you necessarily finish everything one step away before you look at anything two steps away. That gives you breadth-first search, and with it the shortest path in an unweighted graph — for free, purely as a consequence of the ordering.

problemFirst.motivatingProblem: Print a binary tree one level at a time: the root, then both of its children, then all four grandchildren.

bruteForce.idea: Recurse. But recursion goes *deep* first — it will print the whole left subtree before touching the right child, which is the wrong order. You could compute the height, then loop over levels and re-walk the tree once per level to print just that depth.
code: printAtDepth(root, level);   // re-walks the tree from the top every time

complexity.time: O(n·h) — up to O(n²) for a skewed tree

bruteForce.whySlow: Every level re-traverses everything above it. The root is visited h times, its children h-1 times, and so on.

problemFirst.observation: While printing a node, we already hold references to its children. We just need somewhere to park them until the current level is finished.
problemFirst.leap: Park them in a queue. Because children are added at the back and nodes are taken from the front, depth d is always fully processed before depth d+1. One pass, O(n) — and this is exactly breadth-first search.

howItWorks: **offer(x) / add(x)** — put x at the back. O(1).
**poll() / remove()** — take from the front. O(1). `poll` returns null when empty; `remove` throws.
**peek()** — look at the front without removing. O(1).
Naive array implementation: dequeue from index 0 shifts everything left — O(n). Unacceptable.
**Circular buffer** fixes it: keep `head` and `tail` indices and wrap with `(i + 1) % capacity`. Nothing moves; both ends are O(1).
**Deque** (double-ended queue) allows push/pop at both ends — it is a queue and a stack in one class, which is why `ArrayDeque` is the recommended implementation of both.
**PriorityQueue** is a different thing wearing the name: it serves the *smallest* element, not the oldest, in O(log n) via a binary heap.

signals: 'Level by level', 'layer by layer', 'shortest path in an unweighted graph' → BFS with a queue
Processing in arrival order; fairness; scheduling
Buffering between a fast producer and a slow consumer
antiSignals: You need most-recent-first (that is a Stack)
You need highest-priority-first (that is a PriorityQueue)
You need random access by index

implementations.label: Simple
implementations.explanation: A circular-buffer queue. The only interesting line is the modulo: it is what lets the front index move forward forever without any element ever being copied.
code: if (size == items.length) throw new IllegalStateException("queue is full");
if (size == 0) throw new NoSuchElementException("queue is empty");

implementations.label: Optimized
implementations.explanation: Use `ArrayDeque` in real code — it is a growable circular buffer already. The level-order traversal below is the pattern that makes queues worth learning: capturing `q.size()` before the inner loop is what separates one level from the next.
code: int levelSize = q.size();          // freeze the count for THIS level

complexity.time: enqueue O(1) · dequeue O(1) · peek O(1) · search O(n)
complexity.why: Both ends are O(1) only because of the circular indices — a naive 'remove from index 0 and shift' implementation is O(n) per dequeue and turns an O(n) BFS into O(n²). This is the most common hand-rolled-queue bug. `PriorityQueue` differs: its operations are O(log n) because it maintains heap order.

commonMistakes.fix: That is O(n) per removal. Use `ArrayDeque`.

commonMistakes.mistake: Not freezing `q.size()` before the level loop
commonMistakes.fix: The size changes as you enqueue children, so levels bleed into each other. Capture it first.
`PriorityQueue` orders by value, not arrival. Iterating it does not give sorted order either — only repeated `poll()` does.

commonMistakes.mistake: Enqueueing a node without marking it visited
commonMistakes.fix: In graph BFS the same node gets queued many times. Mark visited at enqueue time, not at dequeue time.

realWorldUses: Thread pools and job schedulers hold pending tasks in a queue.
Kafka, RabbitMQ and SQS are queues at the distributed-system scale — same FIFO idea, different failure modes (see the Message Queue lesson).
Network routers buffer packets in queues; the queue length is literally what latency under load measures.
Rate limiters, print spoolers, and request admission control.
interviewNotes: BFS with a queue gives the shortest path in an *unweighted* graph. Say 'unweighted' — for weighted graphs you need Dijkstra, which is BFS with a priority queue.
'Implement a queue using two stacks' is a classic; the amortised O(1) argument is the point of the question.

quiz.question:
enqueue(1); enqueue(2); dequeue(); enqueue(3); dequeue();
Which value was returned by the second dequeue?
quiz.explanation: FIFO: the first dequeue returns 1, leaving [2]; enqueue 3 gives [2,3]; the second dequeue returns 2.

quiz.question: Why does BFS use a queue rather than a stack?
options: FIFO order guarantees all nodes at distance d are processed before any at distance d+1
It does not matter which you use
quiz.explanation: That ordering is what makes the first time you reach a node also the shortest way to reach it. Swap in a stack and you get DFS, which offers no such guarantee.

quiz.question: What is wrong with implementing dequeue as `array.remove(0)` on an ArrayList?
options: It is O(n) because every remaining element shifts left, making BFS O(n²)
It throws on a non-empty list
quiz.explanation: Removing from the front of an array-backed list shifts the whole tail. A circular buffer avoids this by moving an index instead of the data.
